clue.text: Thought to be by Alfred Tennyson initially, but going in to be tested

indicators.note: initially asks for the opening letter of each of the two names Alfred and Tennyson
going in tells us the word but is placed inside the synonym for tested

parts.note: to be tested is to be tried
taken as written

explanation.surface: A poem's authorship is doubtful: it is credited to Tennyson, but must still be checked.
explanation.definitionFit: A work attributed to someone is one thought to be theirs, its authorship assigned but not proven.

clue.text: Formal wear for credit union, perhaps

parts.note: being in credit is being in the black
a tie is a union or bond between two things

explanation.surface: Bankers at a credit union dinner might be expected to dress up formally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' flags that BLACK for credit is an example by way of the phrase 'in the black'.
explanation.definitionFit: Black tie is the dress code of dinner jacket and bow tie, the standard formal evening clothing.

clue.text: Slip out (far from very quietly) of the joint

indicators.note: out suggests the word slip being put out of its proper order

parts.note: taken as written
very quietly is pp (pianissimo) in music; its opposite, very loudly, is ff (fortissimo)

explanation.surface: Someone slips out of a pub, making rather a lot of noise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges SLIP to SPLI; FF is the musical mark for fortissimo, the opposite of pianissimo's PP.
explanation.definitionFit: A spliff is slang for a cannabis cigarette, which is also called a joint.

clue.text: See 22
Spooner's West Midland valley, boring in the extreme

indicators.note: Spooner's signals that the sounds of the two words are swapped, as the Reverend Spooner famously did

parts.note: Dudley is a town in the West Midlands of England
a dale is a valley, especially in northern England

explanation.surface: A guidebook entry dismisses a West Midlands beauty spot as tedious.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the vowel sounds of DUDLEY DALE gives the sound of DEADLY DULL.
explanation.definitionFit: Deadly dull is an idiom for extremely tedious, deadly working as an intensifier.

clue.text: "English animal painter mostly" — now read on

parts.note: a pig is an animal

indicators.note: mostly means only the larger part of the painter's name is kept

parts.note: Raphael was the Italian Renaissance painter

explanation.surface: A book opens by quoting a description of an English painter of animals.
explanation.definitionFit: An epigraph is a quotation at the head of a book or chapter, after which the reader carries on into the text.

clue.text: Someone else the establishment — cavalier lot — won't take 21down 13

parts.note: someone else is literally not me, written not I
CE is the Church of England, the established church

explanation.surface: The arrogant establishment pays no attention to anyone but itself.
explanation.walkthrough: 21down 13 is A BLIND BIT OF, so the definition is the phrase 'won't take a blind bit of ___', said of a cavalier lot.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking no notice means paying no attention, as an offhand or cavalier group would.

clue.text: See 16
Bottomless bowl: covering the rim, a model magnolia

indicators.note: covering means the trimmed bowl surrounds the rim and model
bottomless says the last letter of the word for bowl is dropped

parts.note: a tureen is a deep serving bowl
a lip is the rim of a vessel
the Model T was Ford's famous car, so a model can be T

explanation.surface: A bowl with no base and a model standing on its rim make a strange flower arrangement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottomless' trims the bowl by its last letter; 'a model' is the T of Ford's Model T, a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: The tulip tree is a North American tree of the magnolia family.

clue.text: Reminder about upper class being haughty

indicators.note: about means the reminder goes round the letter for upper class

parts.note: a prod is a nudge or reminder
U denotes upper class in British usage

explanation.surface: A snob reminds us of their upper-class status.
explanation.definitionFit: Proud can mean arrogant or haughty, having too high an opinion of oneself.

clue.text: Row developing in court

indicators.note: developing suggests the letters of in court taking a new shape

explanation.surface: A dispute is brewing in a courtroom.
explanation.definitionFit: A ruction is a noisy disturbance or quarrel, which is a row.

clue.text: Excavate American city without it being 10?

parts.note: to dig is to excavate

indicators.note: without in the old sense of outside: the city's letters go round it

parts.note: NY is New York
taken as written

explanation.surface: Digging up an American city would be beneath one's pride.
explanation.walkthrough: 10 is PROUD, so the definition reads 'being proud'.
explanation.definitionFit: Dignity is a proper sense of self-respect and pride, a state of being proud.

clue.text: See 21 down
See 16
See 21
Takes mikes to get musical effects

indicators.note: effects as in special effects, a rearrangement worked on the letters of takes mikes

explanation.surface: A stage show depends on microphones for its sound effects.
explanation.definitionFit: Kiss Me, Kate is Cole Porter's stage musical based on The Taming of the Shrew.

clue.text: Non-stop adventurous years end: why safety awoke anew

indicators.note: anew means the letters are put together again in a fresh order

explanation.surface: An adventurer ends a wild period of life and wakes up to the value of safety.
explanation.definitionFit: Round the clock every day of the week is an idiom for something never stopping.

clue.text: Constricts outstanding people, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly signals that the word for outstanding people is heard, not seen

parts.note: titans are people of outstanding importance or ability

explanation.surface: A tabloid claims that great figures are restricting freedom.
explanation.definitionFit: To tighten something is to draw it tighter, so tightens means constricts.

clue.text: 13 beef put in, still on the plate, perhaps, without loss

indicators.note: put in tells us the letter goes inside the phrase for leftover food

parts.note: food still on the plate is uneaten

indicators.note: 13 across is bit of, so a bit of beef is its first letter

explanation.surface: A bit of beef is left on the plate untouched.
explanation.walkthrough: 13 is BIT OF, so '13 beef' is a bit of beef, B, put into UNEATEN.
explanation.definitionFit: A team that is unbeaten has suffered no defeats, so it is without a loss.

clue.text: See 23 down
Smitten for batting without scoring?

parts.note: a batsman batting in cricket is in
love is a score of nothing, as in tennis

explanation.surface: A batsman who stays in but never scores is cryptically smitten.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone smitten is infatuated, which is being in love.

clue.text: A pound — I'm not sure where the stamp goes

parts.note: lb is the abbreviation for a pound in weight
um is the sound of hesitation or uncertainty

explanation.surface: A stamp collector is unsure where to put a pound stamp.
explanation.definitionFit: An album is a blank book for a collection, such as a stamp album.

clue.text: The absolutely immaterial won't make a trick, if Dot worked during strike before once losing head

parts.note: a blind is a pretext or trick to deceive

indicators.note: during means the rearranged letters sit within the word for strike

parts.note: biff is an informal word for strike or hit

indicators.note: worked means the letters of if dot are worked into a new order

parts.note: ere is an old word for before

indicators.note: losing head means the first letter of once is removed

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A card player trying to win a trick while a woman named Dot strikes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worked' shuffles 'if Dot', placed 'during' the strike; 'losing head' beheads 'once'. A blind as a trick is a decoy or pretext; the whole phrase means no effect at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that makes not the slightest change is absolutely immaterial; the phrase is an idiom for no effect at all.

clue.text: "Woman of letters" — correspondent? 23down actually

parts.note: a woman of letters can be a writer or someone writing letters; 23down says this French novelist was both

explanation.surface: Is a woman of letters a writer or a correspondent? Actually both.
explanation.walkthrough: 23down is BOTH: the author was a literary woman and also a prolific letter writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Colette was the French novelist, a celebrated woman of letters.

clue.text: Players find press unbreakable

parts.note: the cast is the set of players in a show
to iron clothes is to press them

explanation.surface: Actors discover that a printing press is indestructible.
explanation.definitionFit: Cast-iron is used figuratively of anything firm and unbreakable, such as a cast-iron guarantee.

clue.text: Defence against fighting during Mass?

indicators.note: during means fighting goes inside the word for mass

parts.note: bulk means mass or size
war is fighting

explanation.surface: A church asks whether it is defended while fighting occurs during Mass.
explanation.definitionFit: A bulwark is a defensive wall or rampart, and figuratively any defence.

clue.text: Mary's third keeps dog in order — good news about her and another James?

definitions.text: good news about her and another James?

indicators.note: keeps means the husband's name holds the rearranged letters inside

parts.note: James Hepburn, Earl of Bothwell, was the third husband of Mary, Queen of Scots

indicators.note: order means the letters of dog in are put in a different arrangement

explanation.surface: Mary Queen of Scots' third husband keeps a dog and there is news of mother and baby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'order' rearranges 'dog in', which the husband's title 'keeps'. Mary's son became James VI, so the news is about her and another James.
explanation.definitionFit: Mother and baby both doing well is the stock announcement after a successful birth.

clue.text: See 16
Pressing to include bronze with trigonometric function

indicators.note: to include means the bronze colour goes inside

parts.note: a cogent argument is pressing or compelling
tan is a bronze colour, as of a suntan

explanation.surface: An urgent need to add bronze to a mathematical process.
explanation.definitionFit: The cotangent is the ratio of adjacent to opposite sides, one of the trigonometric functions.
